title: The Evening Brief: Taylor exits a champion as Saturday's games pile up finishes
dek: Katie Taylor closed her career undefeated in front of 80,000 at Croke Park while a full night of games produced walk-offs, milestones, and late controversy across baseball and college football.
author: GoCheckMySports
key_fact: Saturday's biggest story was closure: Taylor's retirement bout and Sanchez's plea motion both moved long-running matters toward an end, while several games turned on final-play officiating calls that remain under review.
bottom_line: Saturday's clearest thread was closure arriving alongside contested endings: Katie Taylor retired undefeated at 26-1 in front of a record Croke Park crowd, and Mark Sanchez moved his stabbing case toward resolution with a guilty plea motion, while Michigan's Hail Mary win and the Rincon cap dispute left officiating and authority questions unresolved. The evidence supports genuine milestones, Taylor's title defense, the Cubs' 200th home run, UMass's historic upset, and equally genuine open disputes, the restored second in Ann Arbor and the SEC's pending Alabama lawsuit against LSU, neither of which the reporting resolves. Watch the Alabama federal court on LSU eligibility, any Big Ten statement on the Michigan clock, MLB's response to the cap incident, and the WNBA's search for Engelbert's successor ahead of a December 31 deadline.
body: Katie Taylor's retirement fight anchors the day. She beat Flora Pili by unanimous decision, 100-90, 100-90, and 98-91, at Croke Park in Dublin on September 5, becoming a three-time undisputed champion and closing her career at 26-1 in front of roughly 80,000 fans, a crowd BBC Sport says was 80 percent first-time boxing attendees. It was the venue's first boxing event since 1972.

Elsewhere the day mixed decisive finishes with disputed ones. Colorado beat Georgia Tech 14-13 after freshman quarterback Julian Lewis threw a go-ahead touchdown with 37 seconds left and the Buffaloes blocked a 45-yard field goal as time expired. UMass ended the nation's longest active losing streak, upsetting Rutgers 37-21 as a 29.5-point underdog, its first win over a Power Four opponent. Oklahoma routed UTEP 51-0 behind three John Mateer touchdown passes and 215 all-purpose yards from Isaiah Sategna.

A cleaner finish drew the sharpest scrutiny. Michigan beat Western Michigan 13-12 after officials restored one second to the clock following a review, allowing Bryce Underwood to connect with JJ Buchanan on a Hail Mary that had initially appeared to fall incomplete at 0:00. Multiple media figures questioned the ruling within hours, and MAC commissioner Jon Steinbrecher has reached out to Big Ten officiating; no official explanation has been released.

Baseball supplied its own share of walk-offs and milestones. Luis Campusano's 10th-inning, two-run homer gave the Padres a 3-2 win over the Yankees, snapping a six-game skid in one-run games and moving San Diego a half-game ahead of Arizona in the NL Wild Card race. The Cleveland Guardians organization recorded four walk-off wins across its affiliates in about three hours on September 4, three of them within minutes of each other. The Cubs reached 200 home runs for the season, first in baseball to do so, on Michael Conforto's milestone shot in a 6-5 win over the Marlins, while reliever Ryan Zeferjahn logged his first save as a Cub. Riley Greene hit two homers and drove in four runs across four straight plate appearances as the Tigers shut out the Guardians 6-0. The Rays placed Shane McClanahan on the 15-day injured list with left forearm tightness, his second IL stint this season.

Off the field, Mark Sanchez filed a motion to plead guilty in Marion Superior Court in an October 2025 stabbing case, days before a September 8 trial date; a sentencing hearing could come November 9 or 16. WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert announced she will retire at the end of 2026 after seven years marked by labor gains, three new franchises, and persistent player criticism over her leadership. Ben Simmons signed a one-year, $3.5 million veteran minimum deal with the Kings, returning after an entire season away rehabilitating back and leg injuries. The Vikings re-signed Harrison Smith for a 15th season on a one-year, $12.25 million deal after Jamal Adams, his intended replacement, tore his knee in the preseason.

The LSU eligibility fight continued. Judge William Jorden ruled LSU may sign players with NFL preseason experience, protecting the school from NCAA and SEC sanctions for now, but the SEC has filed a separate federal lawsuit in Alabama seeking to reverse that protection. And a smaller uniform dispute became a visible protest: after umpire Doug Eddings ordered rookie pitcher Hancel Rincon to straighten his cap during his MLB debut, leading to manager Oliver Marmol's ejection, Cardinals players wore their hats crooked in the dugout the following night, joined by some Rockies players.

The reporting does not explain why the clock was restored in the Michigan game, nor whether MLB will weigh in on Eddings' authority to enforce cap style. Both remain open questions pending further statements.
No desk boards were available this run, so today's numbers rest entirely on the day's reporting.

The coming days carry several concrete checkpoints. The SEC's Alabama federal lawsuit against LSU, coach Lane Kiffin, and athletic director Verge Ausberry will test whether Jorden's protections hold. A judge's decision on Sanchez's plea motion, and a sentencing date of November 9 or 16, will follow the September 8 trial date it was filed to avoid. The WNBA's owners face a December 31 deadline to name Engelbert's successor before she would extend her tenure into 2027. Oklahoma plays Michigan on September 12, a marked step up from UTEP. Zheng Qinwen and Anastasia Potapova both advance in the US Open draw, with Potapova facing seeded Andreeva in the fourth round. And Rincon's cap dispute, along with the Michigan clock review, awaits any word from MLB or the Big Ten on how each was handled.
